stories.topic: Turning Down a Just-Won Nobel Laureate
stories.summary: When Abhijit Banerjee won the Nobel in 2019, his publishers offered him to Amit's podcast for a single hour. Amit said no. He wanted two or three hours minimum (today he'd ask for five) so he could go back before either of them was born and trace, for example, how Abhijit's father Dipak Banerjee had taught Amit's father at Presidency College in the 1960s. The standard one-hour Nobel chat about RCTs would have missed the soul of the man.
stories.insight: Reducing a person to their headline achievement is a kind of intellectual fast food. The interesting threads in any life are the multi-generational ones, and they only surface when you give a conversation enough time to digress.

stories.topic: The Ten-Dollar O-Ring That Killed a $3.2 Billion Shuttle
stories.summary: Michael Kremer's seminal 1993 'O-Ring Theory of Economic Development' takes its name from the 1986 Challenger disaster, where a $10 rubber O-ring failed and destroyed a $3.2 billion vehicle. Kremer's insight isn't the cliche about weakest links: it is that when teams of high-skill people work together, output multiplies rather than adds. Ten people at 0.99 skill yield 9.05; at 0.95, 5.99; at 0.90, only 3.49. A small drop in talent produces a giant drop in output.
stories.insight: This is the math behind why talent clusters and why wages diverge so wildly for what look like small skill gaps. A 0.99 person in a 0.90 team is wasted; a 0.99 person in a 0.99 team is multiplied. The incentives push the best to find each other.

stories.summary: In school and college, Oppenheimer was so miserable and misfitting that he once put poison on his physics teacher's apple. Then he went to Gottingen, was taught by Max Born (who coined the term 'quantum mechanics'), and found himself in classes with Dirac and von Neumann. He transformed entirely.
stories.insight: Talent is contingent on its surroundings. The same person who could not function in one environment becomes a giant in the right one. Congregation does not just train you, it activates you.

stories.topic: The First Paper, Written Without Ever Meeting
stories.summary: Ajay's good friend Achim Zeileis, a statistician in Vienna, struck up a conversation with him and Ila Patnaik on a mailing list, where they realised they were chasing correlated pieces of the same puzzle. They wrote a paper Ajay still considers one of the loveliest of his life entirely on email and SVN, never having met or even video-called. Only afterwards did they meet in person.
stories.insight: Distance work works, but only after the contracting problem is solved. Chance internet collisions can launch real intellectual partnerships, and once the trust is established, the actual labour can be distributed across continents.

stories.summary: Cut off in a remote corner of Tamil Nadu with no access to contemporary mathematics, Ramanujan rebuilt much of 19th-century math from scratch. He never became despondent at being far from Cambridge. The breakthrough came only when he reached Hardy at Cambridge and the world's mathematics flooded in.
stories.insight: Outliers can overcome distance. But for every Ramanujan who escapes obscurity, an unknown number have been lost to it. Outliers should inspire individuals; they should not set policy, because policy is for ordinary talented people who need the cluster.

stories.topic: Anand and the Soviet School of Chess
stories.summary: From the 1930s, the Soviet state taught chess in schools the way other countries taught math. The result was a vast funnel of trained kids and a body of accumulated heuristics so deep that a 1980s Indian player like Devangshu Datta felt as if HSC-level math kids were being thrown against postgraduates: 'we'd struggle through the opening, and in the post-mortem the opponent would say, oh, my trainer taught us that with this structure you have to play this way, and you'd be like shit.' Vishwanathan Anand emerged from this gap, with formative years in the Philippines, no Soviet training, and still became world champion.
stories.insight: Systematic congregation produces a foundational knowledge base, not just better skills. To dominate without it is like 'winning Wimbledon today with a wooden racket.' Anand is a freak; the system is the policy lesson.

stories.topic: Bombay Where Art Comes to Be Corrupted
stories.summary: From a Seen and the Unseen episode with Vikram Sathaye and Roshan Abbas, Amit relays a story about kids who arrive in Bombay from small Maharashtra towns, steeped in Vijay Tendulkar and local cultural forms, brilliant and serious. Within a year of being surrounded by shallow industry talk, the same kid will run into Vikram at a party and say 'dude, how are you doing, let's chill', having lost the deeper register because he developed an inferiority complex about being 'vernie'.
stories.insight: Congregations are not always virtuous. Cities homogenise as much as they aggregate, and a strong cluster of mediocre incentives can corrupt even high-quality talent. The cluster's culture matters as much as its size.

stories.topic: Stage.in and the Bhojpuri Reverse Migration
stories.summary: From Amit's Seen and the Unseen episode with Vinay Singhal: traditional VCs scoffed at a 'Netflix for Bharat' built on dialects (Haryanvi, Bhojpuri, Rajasthani), but Stage.in scaled to roughly 300,000 subscribers and a recent funding round. Vinay told Amit about a 'reverse migration from Bollywood', where Haryanvi kids who would once have boarded the train to become Hindi-film actors now stay home: a Haryanvi industry of around 3,000 people exists.
stories.insight: Technology can rebuild congregations along lines geography never permitted. Urbanisation tends to homogenise dialects out of existence; platforms can selectively reverse that, sustaining sub-cultures that previously had no route to commercial scale.

stories.topic: Visiting the Tibetan Government in Exile
stories.summary: Ajay describes the Tibet Museum in McLeod Ganj, sitting inside a complex of buildings of the Central Tibetan Administration. There is a Department of Home, a Department of Finance, an entire ministerial scaffolding, all funded by donations, with no taxation or coercive power. It looks and behaves like a state, but as an institution it cannot exercise the things that actually define a state.
stories.insight: Play-acting at statehood is poignant but misleading. The real test of state capacity is wielding coercive power decently; you cannot rehearse that with donations and tidy departments. The training wheels for statehood may not be statehood-shaped at all.

stories.topic: Warsaw's Communist HQ Becoming the Stock Exchange
stories.summary: On a visit to Warsaw, Ajay heard the story of how Poland took the largest, most powerful building in the city, the headquarters of the Communist Party, and turned it into the country's stock exchange. The choice was deliberately symbolic, a public declaration that the country had moved on.
stories.insight: Institutions live partly in stone. Re-purposing the symbols of a previous regime is a way of writing the country's new self-understanding into its skyline.

stories.summary: Years ago, before GST came in, Amit wrote an essay on Gandhi's Dandi March. The detail readers found surprising: the tax on salt in independent India ended up far higher than the tax under the British Empire. The very thing Gandhi marched against became more burdensome under our own state.
stories.insight: Freedom from a coloniser is not freedom from extraction. India inherited the colonial state and continued to use it; our freedom struggle, measured against its own grievances, is deeply incomplete.

stories.summary: When India set up the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India, MS Sahoo and Ravi Narain led the writing of an exemplary project plan. It treated the new regulator the way one would treat building a bridge: organisational design, drafting, training, IT systems, layered notification of powers, twenty rounds of review of checks and balances. Then the law was notified anyway, and five people were expected to perform overnight.
stories.insight: India does have the knowledge of how to create a coercive institution properly; it is the discipline to actually use that knowledge that is missing. The IBBI document is a milestone less for what it achieved than for what it proves is possible.

recommendations.item: Why Abhijit Banerjee Had to Go Abroad to Achieve Glory
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's Times of India column on Banerjee's Nobel and the role of Harvard in his trajectory.
recommendations.reason: Sets up the central argument of the episode: Banerjee's Presidency College and JNU years mattered, but it was Harvard, the cluster, that was decisive. The piece introduces Kremer's O-Ring theory as the underlying mechanism.

recommendations.item: The O-Ring Theory of Economic Development
recommendations.creator: Michael Kremer
recommendations.context: Kremer's seminal 1993 paper using the Challenger O-ring as a metaphor for the economics of talent.
recommendations.reason: The mathematical backbone of the cluster argument: 0.99^10 = 9.05, 0.95^10 = 5.99, 0.90^10 = 3.49. Explains why small differences in talent create vast differences in output, why talented people cluster, and why wages diverge so sharply for what look like small skill gaps.

recommendations.creator: Marginal Revolution University
recommendations.context: Tyler Cowen's video walkthrough of Kremer's O-Ring model.
recommendations.reason: Amit recommends it as a clearer-than-his-own explanation of the maths and intuition behind Kremer's paper.

recommendations.item: My Hero, Oppenheimer (Episode 5 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode on Oppenheimer.
recommendations.reason: Background for the Gottingen story: the same misfit who tried to poison his physics teacher became Oppenheimer once placed inside a cluster of giants.

recommendations.item: The Rise of the Creative Class
recommendations.creator: Richard Florida
recommendations.context: Florida's early-2000s book coining the term 'creative class'.
recommendations.reason: An orthogonal but complementary frame to Kremer: economic growth follows where creative congregation happens. Cities full of entrepreneurs, artists, filmmakers, poets, gay and lesbian communities have more openness, more flourishing, and capital then chases the talent. Explains why Bollywood is in Bombay and Silicon Valley exists at all.

recommendations.creator: Jerry Pournelle and Larry Niven
recommendations.context: A science fiction novel containing a passage in which characters debate the persistence of the phrase '20/20 vision' in a world where genetic engineering has made everyone's eyes perfect.
recommendations.reason: Cited as a vivid illustration of skeuomorphism beyond design: how language and convention persist long after the underlying reality has changed. Sets up the episode's opening riff on 'rolling cameras' surviving the death of physical film.

recommendations.item: The Adda at the End of the Universe (Episode 309 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vikram Sathaye and Roshan Abbas
recommendations.context: Amit's year-end episode for 2022.
recommendations.reason: Source of the story about young Maharashtra arrivals losing their depth in Bombay's shallow Bollywood culture. The episode's underlying lesson is that congregations can corrupt as well as elevate.

recommendations.item: The Refreshing Audacity of Vinay Singhal (Episode 291 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vinay Singhal
recommendations.context: Amit's episode on the founder of Stage.in.
recommendations.reason: Source of the 'reverse migration from Bollywood' story and the dialect-led platform model. A counterexample to the homogenising pull of the metropolitan cluster.

recommendations.context: An Indian streaming platform for content in dialects (Haryanvi, Bhojpuri, Rajasthani) rather than just languages.
recommendations.reason: Cited as a real-world demonstration that technology can rebuild congregations along lines that geography wiped out, and that there is real commercial demand for sub-language identities.

recommendations.item: The Tamilian Gentleman Who Took on the World
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's ESPN feature on Vishwanathan Anand.
recommendations.reason: The piece in which Amit first quoted Devangshu Datta's HSC-versus-postgraduate analogy for the gulf between Indian and Soviet-trained chess players. Frames Anand's achievement as 'winning Wimbledon today with a wooden racket'.

recommendations.context: A museum in Dharamshala chronicling the history of Tibet, situated inside the buildings of the Central Tibetan Administration.
recommendations.reason: Ajay encourages everyone to visit. Beyond the artefacts, the experience of walking the lanes of a living, breathing government in exile is the prompt for the entire second-chapter discussion of state capacity, coercive power and the founding of new institutions.

recommendations.item: Building the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India
recommendations.creator: MS Sahoo and Ravi Narain
recommendations.context: The original IBBI project plan: a structured, two-year roadmap for setting up a new regulator with coercive power.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's exhibit for how Indian institutions should be built. Reading it shows that the knowledge exists; the challenge is using it instead of notifying laws and wishing five people into a working agency overnight.

recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on the art and science of economic policy.
recommendations.reason: The argument behind Ajay's hopefulness: bestowing coercive power on an organisation can easily go bad, and the right grand debate is about checks and balances, not about finding 'a better CEO'. India is still stuck at great-man theory; the book is an attempt to push the conversation up a level.

recommendations.creator: George Orwell
recommendations.context: A chronological volume of Orwell's essays rather than his more famous novels.
recommendations.reason: Amit's go-to remedy for writer's block. Reading two or three Orwell essays at random, regardless of subject, frees something in his own writing. Orwell is also a chronological window into a thinker, working out his ideas in real time across decades.

recommendations.creator: George Orwell
recommendations.context: Orwell's classic essay on prose and political clarity.
recommendations.reason: Amit gave it to every young writer he edited. A primer on clear writing and on the moral relationship between honest prose and honest thinking.

recommendations.creator: George Orwell
recommendations.context: Orwell's essay on his motives for writing.
recommendations.reason: Linked in the show notes alongside Orwell's other essays; a companion piece for any reader who wants to understand the writer's relationship to their craft.

recommendations.creator: George Orwell
recommendations.context: Orwell's late essay reviewing Gandhi's autobiography.
recommendations.reason: Amit reads aloud the passage on saints being judged guilty until proved innocent, on Gandhi's vanity, and on the shrewd 'near-saint' inside the saint. A demonstration that Orwell's clarity is not a tic of style but a way of seeing.

recommendations.item: How Cormac McCarthy Became a Copy-Editor for Scientific Books
recommendations.creator: Josh Jones
recommendations.context: An Open Culture piece on the novelist's stint as a copy-editor for scientific manuscripts at the Santa Fe Institute.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's recommendation to every STEM researcher: watch a master of language clean up scientific prose and learn what writing well actually looks like.

recommendations.creator: Deirdre McCloskey
recommendations.context: McCloskey's manual on writing about economics for a lay reader.
recommendations.reason: Amit's standing recommendation for students arriving from sociology or anthropology with a head full of insider jargon. The book applies far beyond economics to any complex subject; its core lesson is that obfuscatory language tends to hide the absence of something to say.

recommendations.context: Amit gestures toward Didion's work as a future, to-be-developed recommendation.
recommendations.reason: Cited as the source of one of his favourite lines about writing: 'I don't know what I think until I write it down.' Didion is held up as a model of writing as self-discovery.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's pre-GST essay on Gandhi's Dandi March and the salt tax.
recommendations.reason: The piece in which he points out that the salt tax under independent India ended up higher than under the British Raj, evidence that our freedom struggle, by its own measure, is unfinished.

recommendations.creator: William Easterly
recommendations.context: Easterly's book on the failures of development economics.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's recommendation builds on the O-Ring conversation: every faddish idea in development has done damage, and Easterly does the first cut of clearing the rubbish. After the clearing, you are left with the real question, 'so what is our theory of growth?' Most modern development philanthropy is still in the grip of the bad ideas Easterly debunks.

recommendations.creator: William Easterly
recommendations.context: Easterly's book on why Western aid efforts have done so much ill and so little good.
recommendations.reason: The one Easterly Amit has actually read. He vouches for it as the work of a clear writer and clear thinker, and as a natural companion volume to The Elusive Quest for Growth.

recommendations.item: What Is the New Chinese Currency Regime?
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah, Achim Zeileis and Ila Patnaik
recommendations.context: The first paper Ajay co-wrote with Zeileis (Vienna) and Patnaik, entirely over email and SVN.
recommendations.reason: Cited not for its content but as Ajay's exhibit for distance-based collaboration done well. It is the proof, in his life, that internet-scale rapport can produce real intellectual work, provided the contracting problem is solved first.

core_ideas.concept: Skeuomorphism and the Persistence of Form
core_ideas.explanation: The producer says 'rolling' even though there are no longer cans of celluloid spinning anywhere. Apple's first books app drew a wooden bookshelf onto an iPhone. Audio software paints physical knobs onto a screen. New technologies are dressed in the clothing of old ones to make users comfortable, but the clothing then survives long after the technology beneath has changed. Steve Jobs' pinch on a screen may itself feel quaint in a hundred years. Convention outlives function.

core_ideas.concept: The Persistence of Bad Conventions: QWERTY
core_ideas.explanation: QWERTY is famously not the optimal way to arrange a keyboard, yet a near-arbitrary 19th century choice has become inescapable. Amit flags this as the harmless face of a bigger pattern: we are stuck inside forms inherited from earlier conditions, even when those conditions no longer apply, and breaking out requires a rare act of intellectual will. He suggests this deserves a book of its own.

Michael Kremer's framework, named for the Challenger disaster's $10 part. When teams perform tasks that are multiplicative in skill, output is roughly the product of individual quality, not their sum. Ten people at 0.99 give 9.05; at 0.95, 5.99; at 0.90, 3.49. Two consequences: small skill gaps create huge wage gaps, and the talented cluster because their value can only be realised in the company of other talented people. A 0.99 person dropped into a 0.90 team is wasted.
core_ideas.quote: A small difference in talent leads to a massive difference in output and productivity.

core_ideas.concept: Two Domains Where Quality Beats Quantity
core_ideas.explanation: Kremer's logic is sharpest in two cases. First, when quality matters more than quantity: one great novelist beats three mediocre ones writing together. Second, when the task has thousands of links and any single failure breaks the whole, like a space shuttle. In both cases the multiplicative structure of output makes congregations of high-skill workers economically inevitable rather than merely nice.

core_ideas.concept: Plug-Compatible Interfaces and the Limits of Remote Work
core_ideas.explanation: Mass manufacturing solved the O-Ring problem in a different way: standardise the parts so any ball bearing is exchangeable for any other. Software does the same with APIs ('the damn thing had better just work'). Where you can engineer plug compatibility, people can be physically separated; where you cannot, they cannot. Movies, where the interfaces between worker and producer are imprecise and personal, sit at the opposite end of the spectrum from APIs and ball bearings, and so resist remote execution.
core_ideas.quote: We are able to achieve great ladders of complexity when we are guaranteed this plug compatibility.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay splits creative work into two phases. Contracting: agreeing what to do, who does what, who decides, how to share the upside. Execution: actually doing the work. The contracting phase needs trust, rapport, in-person banter; humour over text is dangerous; chat-GPT-style prose has no human flavour. Once contracting is done, execution can spread across the world. London, New York and Cambridge are powerful not because the work happens there but because the coalitions form there.

Talent attracts talent, and talent attracts capital, and the resulting cluster is then a virtuous (or vicious) cycle. The mechanism is not only economic; it is psychological. We shape ourselves on the reflections we receive from those around us. To be in a cluster is not just to access information but to internalise the standards, vocabulary, and aspirations of excellence. Amit on Ajay: 'that is why I like to sit with you, because it can only make me a better thinker and a better person.'

Ajay's qualification of the cluster thesis. In STEM, problems are universal and you can play a global game from a small town if you have the internet. In humanities and social sciences, authenticity is decisive. To know Indian economics, you must be in India because every conversation, every street scene, every glance feeds the intuition. Being abroad, Ajay felt 'a certain emptiness' from being away from his subject. Bollywood films must be made in Bombay for the same reason.

Ramanujan and Anand are paraded as proof that genius transcends geography. Amit pushes back: yes, exceptional minds can overcome distance, but they are exceptions. For every Ramanujan who reached Hardy, an unknown number have been lost. Outliers should comfort individuals but never set policy. Policy must serve ordinary talented people who do need the cluster.

core_ideas.concept: Sturgeon's Law: 99% of Everything Is Crap
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's pushback on Amit's lament about Bombay. Yes, most of Bollywood is crass and shallow, but so is most of the Indian startup world, most of Silicon Valley, most of everything. Sturgeon's Law is a useful corrective against romanticising any cluster. The signal in clusters comes from the top sliver; the noise is the bulk.

You don't need a Bollywood-scale agglomeration to do creative work, but you cannot make a movie with three people either. There is a minimum economy of scale below which certain projects are impossible. Pune may have an engineering culture even if Bhopal does not. The cluster question is not 'is bigger better' but 'is it big enough'.

Within India, bright engineers from the Hindi heartland flee to Bangalore, Pune, Bombay, Madras, Hyderabad and Kerala. That is centripetal pull. But not all of them go on to Silicon Valley; the pull weakens with distance. Amit's complementary insight is that technology and capitalism can also enable centrifugal flows, sustaining sub-cultures (Stage.in's dialect content, Haryanvi cinema) that pure agglomeration would have homogenised away.

core_ideas.concept: Brain Drain Is a Question About Us
core_ideas.explanation: The old talk in India was 'brain drain': our IIT kids go abroad. Amit reframes the question. Each individual is making a perfectly rational choice for themselves; the right question is why we are unable to build centres of excellence here that they would prefer not to leave. We are still, today, chasing good people away. The answer requires building the conditions for clusters to form, in Florida's sense and Kremer's.

core_ideas.concept: Government in Exile as Wannabe State
core_ideas.explanation: The Central Tibetan Administration in McLeod Ganj has departments of finance and home, ministerial scaffolding, the appearance of statehood. But it has no taxation, no coercive power; it is a philanthropic organisation funded by donations. Ajay's verdict: no amount of these tidy structures is real training for the problem of coercive power. They may even induce a complacent isomorphic mimicry, the belief that one is ready when one is not. You only learn to handle coercive power by handling it.

Across the great post-colonial experiment, by and large, new states worked out badly, and worked out worst when freedom came through armed struggle. Violence changes the people who win and the people they raise to lead them; military generals are rarely philosopher kings. India's near-miracle was Gandhi's ahimsa, which kept that particular failure mode at bay.

East Germany did best because it inherited the entire West German institutional package overnight; even so, the gap with West Germany has not closed. The Baltics and most of Eastern Europe also flourished because they had lived under communism and wanted to flee it, and because EU accession came with twenty thousand pages of binding draft law. They could not make certain mistakes. Russia is the catastrophic counter-case: economic shock therapy with no comparable attention to the state, and freedom never coded into laws and institutions. Hungary is still doing badly; Poland medium-bad.

core_ideas.concept: Liberal Democracy Is More Than Elections
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's drumbeat: liberal democracy is not merely voting every five years. It is constitutionalism, constitutional morality, the rule of law, checks and balances, and the cultivated sensibility through which a certain kind of person bubbles up into power. East Germany got this on a red carpet. We are still figuring it out.

core_ideas.concept: The Bridge Analogy for New Institutions
core_ideas.explanation: India accepts that a bridge takes years: project plan, design, drafting, training, IT, ribbon-cutting at the end. We should treat coercive new institutions the same way. The IBBI project plan by MS Sahoo and Ravi Narain is the closest we came: a structured two-year process of organisation design, drafting, training, IT, twenty rounds of review of checks and balances, then phased notification of powers. Instead the law was notified anyway and five people were expected to perform on day one.

Ajay's metaphor for the Indian state. Coercive power is a nuclear reactor; without enough cladding (well-drafted laws, judicial branch, constitutional protections) it irradiates everyone. Most Indian laws are written on optimistic readings of human beings and recklessly confer arbitrary power. The DNA of an institution lies in its founding law, and bad DNA produces self-perpetuating decay: discretionary power attracts the wrong people, who then write the next law worse.

When an Indian agency fails, our reflex is to demand a better CEO. Ajay calls this a primitive theory. The right debate is about checks and balances, about the structural conditions under which any holder of the role would behave decently. Public choice theory is the missing intellectual piece. India is still pre-public-choice in its institutional imagination.

The standard claim is that clear thinking produces clear writing. Amit (and Orwell) insist on the opposite direction too: forcing yourself to write clearly forces you to think clearly, because clear language strips away the jargon and abstraction in which fuzzy thoughts hide. Writing is research, not its byproduct. Joan Didion: 'I don't know what I think until I write it down.' Whenever Amit reads obfuscatory prose he assumes the writer is full of shit.

core_ideas.concept: Good Prose Should Be a Window Pane
core_ideas.explanation: Orwell's image, sometimes invoked as a definition of the goal of writing. The reader looks through, not at, the language; the words disappear in service of the thought. Used here as a shared standard for podcast conversation as much as prose, and as the criterion by which Amit judges the obfuscatory writing of academia.

core_ideas.concept: Saints Should Be Judged Guilty Until Proved Innocent
core_ideas.explanation: Orwell's opening posture in 'Reflections on Gandhi'. The questions to ask of any saint are about vanity, about the consciousness of being a humble naked old man shaking empires, about the compromises of entering politics, which are inseparable from coercion and fraud. Even after asking them all, Orwell concludes there was a shrewd, able person inside Gandhi who could have been a brilliant lawyer or businessman. The frame is a model for skeptical, fair-minded biography of any public figure.
core_ideas.quote: Saints should always be judged guilty until they are proved innocent.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's optimism is structural. A century ago, the chattering classes argued about a hypothetical free India, and they got many things wrong, especially their belief that the state would be led by good people like Gandhi and Nehru. Today's R&D phase is figuring out what a successful, prosperous India looks like, what checks and balances, what laws, what institutions. When the public outcry comes that some agency has failed, the country needs a community already equipped with the answers.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay on the 'rolling' word: a thousand years from now we may still be saying 'rolling' to start filming, even though there will not have been a film canister anywhere within human memory. The producer Vartika is the proximate cause.
Ajay's deadpan reduction of Everything is Everything: 'a YouTube podcast with an eclectic name, everything is everything.' Said while explaining that you can't make a movie with a team this small.

Amit, after Ajay says you can't make a movie with three people: 'You just kind of made [Vartika] feel so bad.' Vartika, off camera, that 'it's a three-man team and we couldn't have made a movie even if we wanted to.'

Devangshu Datta on the Indian-Soviet chess gap, quoted by Amit: in the post-mortem the East European opponent would explain the structure he had been taught as a child, 'and you'd be like, shit. Which me [...] they were playing.'
Amit on academic prose: 'Whenever I read [some]thing full of obfuscatory language, I know that person is full of shit.'
Amit hoping to outlive his heroes: he notes Bastiat and Orwell both died at 49, his current age. 'May I somehow reach the end of December.'

Amit, on India under independence: 'the tax on salt at the time, and I'm sure even today with GST, was far more in independent India than it was under the British Empire.' Gandhi marched against the lesser tax.

'As every Russian schoolboy knows' — the chess world's inside phrase for things that look deep and arcane to outsiders but are common knowledge to a Soviet-trained child. Has since travelled into many other domains as shorthand for the gulf systematic congregation creates.
'Winning Wimbledon today with a wooden racket' — Amit's image for Anand becoming chess world champion without the Soviet training base.
Sturgeon's Law: ninety-percent (or more) of everything is crap. Invoked by Amit and Ajay to deflate the romanticism around Bollywood, Silicon Valley, and the Indian startup scene alike.

Skeuomorphism: the design term for new technology dressed in the clothing of older technology (digital books on a wooden bookshelf, knobs on a recording app). Used as the lens for the episode's opening on 'rolling cameras'.

Nikolai Krylenko, the Soviet functionary who allegedly declared 'we must finish once and for all with the neutrality of chess... the formula chess for the sake of chess.' Stalin had him purged in 1938. The intellectual founder of the chess-as-state-instrument doctrine.
Fischer-Spassky 1972 (Amit misremembers as 1973) as the seminal Cold War chess match: an American genius breaking Soviet hegemony in a discipline they had built into a national instrument.
Charles de Gaulle's Free France in London during WWII, contrasted with the Tibetan government in exile: de Gaulle did not bother setting up a department of health; he focused on freeing France.
The Warsaw Communist Party HQ becoming the Polish stock exchange after 1989, as a public statement of regime change.
Jeffrey Sachs and Russia's shock-therapy liberalisation, invoked as the cautionary tale of economic reform without state-building.
The University of Chicago in its early years, deliberately distant from the East Coast establishment and richer in independence of thought because of it.
'Vernie' — the pejorative urban Indian term for the vernacular speaker, against which the episode argues. Cities homogenise the dialects out of even talented small-town arrivals.
Joan Didion's line, paraphrased by Amit: 'I don't know what I think until I write it down.' Used as the manifesto for writing as discovery.

Cormac McCarthy as a copy-editor at the Santa Fe Institute, cleaning up scientific manuscripts. Ajay's recommended reading for any STEM researcher who wants to see what good prose actually looks like.

Orwell on Gandhi: 'inside the saint, or near-saint, there was a very shrewd, able person who could, if he had chosen, have been a brilliant success as a lawyer and administrator, or perhaps even a businessman.' Read aloud by Amit.
